etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 御 (o-, honorific prefix, kun'yomi) +‎ 宅 (taku, “home”, on'yomi).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 御(お) (o-, honorific prefix) + 邪(じゃ)魔(ま) (jama, “nuisance, bother”) + します (shimasu, formal of する (suru), “to do”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Probably from Dutch Azië.
Kanji form from Chinese 亞細亞 / 亚细亚 (Yàxìyà)

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Borrowed from French gramme or English gramme, gram. Original form was ガラム (garamu) (compare to ガラス (garasu) and グラス (gurasu)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Borrowed from English glam.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Etymology tree
Arabic قَهْوَة (qahwa)bor.
Ottoman Turkish قهوه (kahve)bor.
Italian caffèbor.
Dutch koffiebor.
▲
English coffeeinflu.

Borrowing from Dutch koffie, also influenced by English coffee, ultimately from Arabic قَهْوَة (qahwa). Doublet of カフェ (kafe) and カフワ (kafuwa).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese.
Compound of 三日 (mika, “third day of a lunar month”) +‎ 月 (tsuki, “moon”). The tsuki changes to zuki as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Probably a semantic shift from 端 (heta, “edge of something”), referring metaphorically to the edge of one's abilities or knowledge.
The kanji spelling appears to be an instance of jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
Compound of 下 (shita, “down; under; lower”) +‎ 手 (te, “hand”).
Occasionally encountered with rendaku (連濁), where the -te ending changes to -de.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Compound of 下 (shimo, “lower”) +‎ 手 (te, “hand”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: Compound of 下り (kudari, “descending”, the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of verb 下る (kudaru, “to descend, to go down”)) +‎ 手 (te, “hand; side, direction”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 5
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 下手 (MC haeX|haeH syuwX).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 人(ひと) (hito, “person”) + 込(こ)み (komi, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 込(こ)む (komu, “to go into, be full of, have a lot of”).).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Apparently coined in Japanese from Middle Chinese-derived elements, as a compound of 体 (tai, “body”) +‎ 操 (sō, “control, manipulate”). First cited in education-related materials from the early Meiji Period in the early 1870s, as part of educational reforms that included the addition of physical education to school curricula.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Compound of 髪 (kami, “hair on the head”) +‎ 剃り (sori, “shaving facial hair or body hair; a shaver”, the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 剃(そ)る (soru, “to shave facial hair or body hair”).). First cited in the ten-volume Wamyō Ruijushō of 934 CE.
The kanji are from Chinese 剃刀 (tìdāo).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 博物 (hakubutsu, “wide learning”) +‎ 館 (kan, “building”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese compound 國民 (MC kwok mjin).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Compound of native Japanese words: 国 (kuni, “country”) +‎ 民 (tami, “people”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Compound of 女 (onna, “a woman; female”) +‎ の (no, appositional particle) +‎ 子 (ko, “a child”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
Compound of 女 (me, “a woman; female”) +‎ の (no, appositional particle) +‎ 子 (ko, “a child”).
Less commonly used than onnanoko above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 姓名 (MC sjengH mjieng, literally “surname, clan name + name, given name”). The reading is kan'on, so likely a later borrowing. Compare modern Min Nan reading sèⁿ-miâ.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
/siaumiau/ → /ɕjɔːmjɔː/ → /ɕoːmjoː/
From Middle Chinese 姓名 (MC sjengH mjieng, literally “surname, clan name + name, given name”). The goon, so likely the initial borrowing. Compare modern Hakka reading siang-miàng.
Rare in modern Japanese. Largely superseded by the seimei reading above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Compound of 姓 (kabane, “clan”) +‎ 名 (na, “name”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 寝 (ne, “sleeping”, the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “the continuative or stem form”) of verb 寝る (neru, “to sleep”)) +‎ 坊 (bō, “boy”, term of endearment).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 平 (hira, “flat, smooth”) +‎ 仮名 (kana). The kana changes to gana as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
/bentau/ → /bentɔː/ → /bentoː/.
Probably a variant of 面(めん)筒(とう) (mentō, “(obsolete) tub for distributing portions of food”), from 面(めん) (men, “face”) + 筒(とう) (tō, “bucket, tub”) (originally referring to a tub for washing the face), both from Middle Chinese.
The use of 弁 for ben is an example of phonetic ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)), due to 便 having another sense of “human excrement”.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Shift from 弁(べん)当(とう) (bentō) above, shortening the vowel.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 受ける (ukeru, “to receive”) +‎ 賜る (tamawaru, “to be granted”), with alternative (irregular) spelling as 受け賜る.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: 方 (“direction”) +‎ 針 (“needle”), another name for the 磁針 (jishin, “magnetic needle”), with the meaning figuratively extending to "guidance" in general.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Compound of 毛 (ke, “fur, body hair”) +‎ 皮 (kawa, “skin, pelt”). The kawa changes to gawa as an instance of rendaku (連濁).
First cited to a work from 1690, but possibly older, considering the mid-1200s appearance of Chinese-derived homograph 毛皮 (mōhi). This kegawa reading appears to have mostly superseded the mōhi reading.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
Ultimately from Middle Chinese 毛皮 (MC maw|mawH bje).
First cited to the 正法眼蔵 (Shōbōgenzō), a collection of works dated 1231­–53 and written by the 13th century Japanese Buddhist monk and founder of the Sōtō Zen school, Eihei Dōgen.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Probably from 破手 (hade, “breaking melody”, in reference to a lively style of samisen playing), or possibly a shift from haede, as a compound of 映え (hae, “shining; glory”, the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of verb 映える (haeru, “to shine; to be glorious, to be outstanding”)) +‎ 手 (te, “hand; style, way, state”). The te changes to de as an instance of rendaku (連濁).
Appears from the late 1600s.
The use of the 派 character is an example of ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 消し (keshi, “erasing”, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 消(け)す (kesu, “put out, extinguish; erase”)) +‎ ゴム (gomu, “rubber”, from Dutch gom).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Related to 空(むな)しい (munashī, “empty”). The kanji are ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)).
(This etymology is missing or incomplete. Please add to it, or discuss it at the Etymology scriptorium.)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
目(め) (me, “eye”) + 立(た)つ (tatsu, “to stand”).
The tatsu changes to datsu as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Compound of 素(しろ) (shiro, “plain, undecorated”) + 人(うと) (-uto, “person”).
The term 人 (hito, “person”) appears in various older compounds with a root form of 人 (*puto → *buto → *udo, *puto → *futo → *uto). This form is never seen in isolation, and it often undergoes further phonetic changes to combine with preceding vowels. Compare the formation of 仲人 (nakōdo), from naka + udo; 旅人 (tabiudo), from tabi + udo.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Given the mixed Sinitic-Japanese reading, probably coined in Japan as a compound of 職 (shoku, “employment, trade, job”, on'yomi, from Middle Chinese) +‎ 場 (ba, “place, site”, kun'yomi, from Old Japanese).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
⟨mi2 tu kara⟩ → */mʷɨdukara/ → /mid͡zukara/ → /mizukara/
Originally a compound of 身 (mi, “body”) +‎ つ (tsu, Old Japanese possessive particle) +‎ 柄 (kara, “quality, characteristic → by itself”).
The okurigana ら (ra) is used to indicate the reading.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: (This term, 自ら, is an alternative spelling of the above term.)

etymologies.text:
⟨yukupe1⟩ → */jukupʲe/ → /jukuɸe/ → /jukuwe/ → /jukue/
From Old Japanese.
From verb 行く (yuku, “to go”) +‎ 辺 (-he, “direction, location”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Alteration of 迷い子 (mayoigo). The ko changes to go as an instance of rendaku (連濁).
